solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Play recording back to new parent

indicators.note: back tells us to read the recording's two letters the other way round

parts.note: EP is an extended-play record

indicators.note: new signals that the letters of parent are made fresh, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone plays a recording in reverse to a parent who has just had a baby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns EP into PE; 'new' rearranges PARENT into TERPAN.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. Barrie's stage play about the boy who never grows up carries this title.

clue.text: Post about a King Lear character

indicators.note: about means the post goes round the other piece

parts.note: a post is a pole stuck in the ground
B. B. King, the blues guitarist, gives the initials BB

explanation.surface: Something is posted about one of the figures in Shakespeare's King Lear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King Lear' looks like Shakespeare's play, but 'a King' is B.B. King and the definition is just 'Lear character', from Edward Lear's nonsense verse.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pobble Who Has No Toes is a nonsense poem by Edward Lear, so this creature is one of his characters.

clue.text: Smart clothing draped over back of the seats

indicators.note: in a down clue the clothing lies on top of the next piece, as if hung over it

parts.note: a jacket, waistcoat and trousers in matching cloth make a formal three-piece suit

indicators.note: back of points to the final letter of the word the

explanation.surface: Fancy clothes have been thrown over the back of the chairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draped over' puts the suit above E, the last letter of 'the', in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A sofa and two matching armchairs sold as a set make up this furniture, so it is a group of seats.

clue.text: Smells Europeans first off

indicators.note: first off says the opening letter is dropped from the word for Europeans

parts.note: Greeks are people from Greece, so Europeans

explanation.surface: Smells from Europeans come first, then someone sets off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first off' takes the G from GREEKS.
explanation.definitionFit: To stink or give off a strong unpleasant odour is to smell, the verb in its third-person form.

clue.text: Wasting an award

parts.note: an gives the single letter A
an award such as a cup or shield won in competition

explanation.surface: Getting a prize is called a waste of time.
explanation.definitionFit: Muscles that waste away through disuse undergo this decline, a noun naming the wasting itself.

clue.text: Grab one by the lapels?

definitions.meaning: to seize or arrest someone, as police do
the part of a jacket or shirt round the neck, sitting next to the lapels

explanation.definitionFit: Police slang uses this verb for nabbing a suspect, and it is also the neckband of a garment beside its lapels.

clue.text: Where Parisian set off in boat

parts.note: ou is the French word for where, as a Parisian would say it
to trigger something is to set it off

explanation.surface: Someone asks where a man from Paris set off on a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A canoe with a float on a projecting frame for stability is a craft of this type, so a kind of boat.

clue.text: Man with lunchbox dressed in filthier cords

indicators.note: dressed means prepared or arranged, so the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A man carrying his lunch is wearing particularly grubby corduroy trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dressed' rearranges IN plus FILTHIER CORDS. 'Lunchbox' was the British tabloid nickname for the sprinter's bulge in his tight Lycra shorts.
explanation.definitionFit: The British Olympic 100m champion was nicknamed for his 'lunchbox' by the tabloids, so he is that man.

clue.text: Notice put up during rubbish motor trial

indicators.note: during says the notice and the turned word go inside the word for rubbish

parts.note: rot means nonsense or rubbish
AD is short for advertisement, a notice

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word for put is read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: to set something down is to put it

explanation.surface: A sign goes up while a hopeless car is being tested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses the word for put, in this down answer; 'during' places both pieces inside the word for rubbish. 'Notice put up' reads like one phrase for a posted sign, but 'put' gives its own letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Testing a car by driving it on public roads is a standard trial of a motor vehicle.

clue.text: Raincoat, British, worn by the Queen in northern town

indicators.note: in says these letters go inside the name of the town

parts.note: Bury is a town near Manchester in northern England

indicators.note: worn by means the British letters wrap round the royal initials, like a coat on its wearer

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: The Queen wears a British raincoat while visiting a northern town.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury is a town in Greater Manchester. 'worn by' has the British letters wrap round the royal initials, as a coat wraps its wearer.
explanation.definitionFit: This British fashion house is famed for its trench coats, so its name stands for a raincoat.

clue.text: Lines created as result of sunbathing in southern South Africa

indicators.note: in says the colour from the sun goes inside the other letters

parts.note: ZA is the international code for South Africa
a suntan is what sunbathing creates

explanation.surface: Poems were written after lying in the sun in the south of South Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of lines forming a unit of a poem is a verse, so the definition names it by its lines.

clue.text: Organist's choice of second jumper?

parts.note: a top is a garment such as a jumper or sweater

explanation.surface: An organist chooses a second pullover.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'jumper' in Britain is a pullover sweater, not someone who jumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Organists pull knobs that select ranks of pipes, so each one is a choice of sound.

clue.text: Journalist in the French city

indicators.note: in places the journalist inside the French article

parts.note: les is the French plural word for the
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A reporter is in a French city.
explanation.walkthrough: Leeds is a large city in Yorkshire, northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: This large Yorkshire place is a city in northern England.

clue.text: Slip found in Room at the Top, not initially an element in fuel added to the fire

indicators.note: in says the trimmed room and the element go inside the fuel

parts.note: peat is dug turf burnt as fuel on a fire

indicators.note: not initially drops the opening letter of the top room

parts.note: an attic is the room at the top of a house
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen, an element

explanation.surface: A slip is found in a copy of the novel Room at the Top, and coal is thrown on the fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Room at the Top' looks like the title of John Braine's novel, but here it is simply the top room of a house, losing its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip is a woman's undergarment, and this skirt-like underlayer is one.

clue.text: Set fire to a city catalogue

parts.note: lit means set fire to
NY is New York, a city

explanation.surface: Someone burns a list of a city's buildings.
explanation.definitionFit: A long recited list, such as a catalogue of complaints, is this kind of repetitive enumeration.

clue.text: Genuine description of some nautical characters

indicators.note: the answer, split into parts, is read as a description of a stretch of the letters that follow

parts.note: characters means letters, here the letters of the word nautical, where the second and third are followed by the fourth to sixth

explanation.surface: Something truly describes a set of seafaring folk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nautical characters' suggests sailors, but means the letters of the word NAUTICAL, where AU is followed by TIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Something real and not fake is the true article, so genuine.

clue.text: Somewhat resembles a dog appearing around temples

indicators.note: around tells us to turn those letters round
somewhat says only part of the run of words is used

explanation.surface: Something looks a bit like a dog when it shows up near places of worship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat' picks SADOGAP from 'resembleS A DOG APpearing'; 'around' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiered towers built in East Asia as Buddhist shrines are temples, plural like the answer.

clue.text: Foremost of boats certainly not first to go to be launched

indicators.note: foremost of picks the opening letter of boats

parts.note: the one at the end is certainly not the first
off means going, as in 'they're off'

explanation.surface: The lead boat, certainly not the first to leave, is launched.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's boats being launched suggests ships, but the answer is a rocket's lift-off.
explanation.definitionFit: A rocket taking off from its pad leaves the ground, so this verb phrase means to be launched.

clue.text: Found small animal in large dictionary

indicators.note: in places the pet inside the other letters

parts.note: OED is the Oxford English Dictionary
a cat is a small animal

explanation.surface: A small creature was discovered inside a big dictionary.
explanation.definitionFit: Found in the sense of discovered or tracked down, past participle like the answer.

clue.text: Queen singer was an idler?

definitions.meaning: the legendary Queen of Carthage in Virgil's Aeneid
the British pop singer of the album No Angel

explanation.definitionFit: The Carthaginian queen and the pop star share the name, and someone who did nothing 'did O'.

clue.text: Bed a woman

parts.note: a berth is a sleeping bunk on a ship or train

explanation.surface: Someone takes a woman to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a woman's given name, so it can stand for a woman.

clue.text: Boy's first impulse regarding snowball

indicators.note: first picks the opening letter of the boy's word

parts.note: an urge is an impulse
on means regarding, as in a talk on poetry

explanation.surface: A boy's first instinct concerns throwing a snowball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snowball' looks like a noun for a boy's game but is the verb: to grow rapidly.
explanation.definitionFit: To snowball is to grow quickly, and to flourish or expand in that way is to sprout and grow.

clue.text: Couples put a little cash in Scottish banks

indicators.note: in places the coin inside the Scottish word

parts.note: braes are hillsides or banks in Scottish usage
C stands for a cent, a small coin

explanation.surface: Someone deposits a small amount of money in Scotland's banks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banks' suggests financial institutions, but BRAES are Scottish hillsides.
explanation.definitionFit: A brace is a pair, as in a brace of pheasants, so the plural means couples.

clue.text: One that supports stocking revolutionary American poet

indicators.note: revolutionary means turning over, so the abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: Stephen Spender was an English poet

explanation.surface: Someone who backs stockpiling is a radical American poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stocking' looks like stockpiling goods, but it is the hosiery a garter belt holds up.
explanation.definitionFit: A strap fixed to a garter belt holds up a stocking, so it is something that supports it.

clue.text: Drought results in English river primarily being this?

definitions.text: Drought results in English river primarily being this?

indicators.note: primarily picks the first letters of the words before it

explanation.surface: A drought leaves an English river less wet than before.
explanation.walkthrough: The initial letters of the first five words give the answer, and the whole clue describes what a drought does to a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A river in a drought holds less water, so it becomes more arid than before.

clue.text: Physicist sporting cardi

indicators.note: sporting is read as playing about with the letters of cardi

explanation.surface: A scientist is wearing a cardigan.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'cardi' is British slang for a cardigan.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Dirac was the British theoretical physicist who predicted antimatter.

clue.text: Drug ring — very good one, note

parts.note: O is shaped like a ring
PI is short for pious, very good
A means one
TE is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A drugs gang gets a very good tip.
explanation.definitionFit: Morphine and other narcotics from the poppy are drugs of this class.

clue.text: Obsessive barking routine by Crufts beginner

indicators.note: barking means mad, so the letters of routine go crazy
beginner picks the first letter of Crufts

explanation.surface: A newcomer to the Crufts dog show has a routine of barking.
explanation.walkthrough: Crufts is Britain's famous dog show, which fits 'barking'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone anxious and fixated is obsessive, adjective like the answer.

clue.text: European to pull female for wife

indicators.note: for says the female letter replaces the wife letter

parts.note: to wrench is to pull hard

explanation.surface: A European tries to seduce a woman in place of his wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pull' looks like British slang for picking up a partner, but it gives WRENCH.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from France is a European.

clue.text: Heard robbers? Drat!

indicators.note: heard says the word for thieves is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: nickers are people who nick, British slang for steal

explanation.surface: Someone hears there are robbers and swears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knickers!' is a mild British exclamation of annoyance.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of irritation, used in British speech like 'drat' or 'damn'.
